mainTopic: Defining a lost item, protecting land, and what the Torah's doubled verbs teach about returning, sending away, rebuking, unloading and loading
overview: The amud opens with the end of a ברייתא about which found items count as lost. It ends with a rule that one must block floodwater heading for someone's field. רבא learns from 'all lost items' that protecting land is part of השבת אבידה. He rejects רב חנניא's proof from the floodwater case, because it may be about sheaves that still need the ground. The גמרא then finds a contradiction in the משנה about animals running or grazing on the road and in vineyards. אביי's answer is rejected, and רבא resolves it: for running, it depends which way the animal faces, and for grazing, the difference is loss of the animal versus damage to the land. Next, רבא explains doubled verbs like השב תשיבם, שלח תשלח and הוכח תוכיח: the first word means 'even a hundred times' and the second widens the מצוה. The amud closes by asking why the Torah needed separate verses for unloading, loading and returning a lost item, and that answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the list: which found items count as lost
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes its list. An animal in danger or out of place counts as an אבידה. Items that seem placed on purpose do not, unless they stay there three days in a row.
steps.simpleTranslation: A donkey with its gear overturned on a main road, or a cow running through vineyards, is a lost item. A cloak next to a fence, an ax next to a fence, or a cow grazing among vineyards is not a lost item. But if they are there three days in a row, it is a lost item.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא that sorts found items into 'lost' and 'not lost'. This picks up in the middle of a sentence that started before this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is whether the situation shows the owner lost control. A running cow or an overturned load signals trouble, while a cloak by a fence looks deliberately set down. Seeing the item in the same place three days in a row changes the picture: now it looks forgotten.

keyTerms.meaning: A main public road or highway
A lost item that one must take and return

steps.confusionAlert: A cow 'running' (רָצָה) in vineyards is lost, but a cow 'grazing' (רוֹעָה) in vineyards is not. One word changes the ruling, so read carefully.

phrases.english: on a main road, or a cow running among the vineyards
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from before: a donkey with its gear overturned on a main road.

phrases.english: this is a lost item.
A cloak at the side of a fence,
an ax at the side of a fence,
or a cow grazing among the vineyards
this is not a lost item.
If it is there three days one after another
this is a lost item.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Signs of trouble make an item an אבידה. Items that look placed on purpose are not, unless they stay three consecutive days.

steps.title: Water about to flood a field
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא adds that if someone sees water rushing toward another person's field, he must put up a barrier to block it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he sees water flowing and coming toward a field, he must build a barrier in front of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds one more case: blocking floodwater to protect someone else's field. The next steps will argue about exactly what this case proves.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here nothing has been 'found'. The duty is to prevent a loss before it happens. Steps 4–7 discuss whether the loss being prevented is the land itself or something lying on the land.

keyTerms.meaning: Builds a barrier in front of them

phrases.english: If he saw water that is flowing and coming
he must build a barrier in front of it.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: One must block floodwater threatening another's field.

steps.title: רבא: protecting land is part of returning lost items
steps.stepSummary: רבא learns from the word 'all' in the פסוק that השבת אבידה includes preventing loss of someone's land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: 'With all lost items of your brother' comes to include the loss of land.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא makes a new statement. The extra word 'all' (לְכׇל) in the פסוק adds land to the מצוה of returning lost things.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land cannot get lost in the usual sense, since it doesn't move. So רבא needs an extra word in the פסוק to teach that harm to land, such as flooding, is also something we must prevent.

keyTerms.meaning: To include (learned from an extra word)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the rest of the discussion: is there a source that agrees with רבא that land is included?

phrases.english: Rava said: "With every lost item of your brother"
phrases.notes: דברים 22:3

phrases.english: this comes to include the loss of land.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: The word 'all' in the פסוק adds loss of land to השבת אבידה.

steps.title: רב חנניא brings support from the flooding case
steps.stepSummary: רב חנניא tells רבא that the ברייתא about blocking floodwater supports his view.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חנניא said to רבא: There is a ברייתא that supports you: if he sees water flowing and coming, he must build a barrier in front of it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חנניא tries to prove רבא right using the flooding case from step 2.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reasoning is that blocking floodwater protects the field itself. If the ברייתא requires this, it seems land is included in השבת אבידה, just as רבא said.

phrases.english: Rav Chananya said to Rava:
There is a teaching that supports you:
If he saw water that is flowing and coming
he must build a barrier in front of it.

steps.raayaObject: רבא's rule that loss of land is included
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא requiring one to block floodwater from a field

steps.title: רבא rejects the proof: the case is about sheaves
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the ברייתא does not help him, because it is talking about a field with sheaves lying in it. The water would ruin the sheaves, not the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: If it is because of this, it does not support me. What case are we dealing with here? Where there are sheaves in the field.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא himself turns down the support. He explains that the ברייתא could be talking about protecting sheaves, not land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sheaves are movable objects, and those are clearly covered by השבת אבידה. So the ברייתא might have nothing to do with land, and it cannot prove רבא's point.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not taking back his own rule. He only says this particular ברייתא is not proof for it.

phrases.english: He said to him: If it is because of this,
don't support me with it.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets, but the corrected wording is the word in square brackets, meaning 'support me'.

phrases.english: What are we dealing with here?
Where there are sheaves in the field.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the support offered in step 4
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the proof from this ברייתא; רבא's rule still stands
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be read as protecting movable sheaves, not the land itself

steps.title: If it's about sheaves, why say it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if the case is about sheaves, protecting them is obvious, so why would the ברייתא need to teach it?
steps.simpleTranslation: If there are sheaves there, what is the point of saying it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's new reading, saying it makes the ברייתא teach something obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sheaves are ordinary movable property, which everyone agrees must be protected. A ברייתא shouldn't need to tell us something so simple, so רבא's reading seems weak.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the point of saying it? (It's obvious)

phrases.english: If there are sheaves,
what is there to say? It's obvious!

steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's explanation that the ברייתא is about sheaves
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Protecting movable sheaves is obvious, so the ברייתא would be teaching nothing new

steps.title: The sheaves still need the ground
steps.stepSummary: The case is sheaves that still need the ground to dry. One might think they count like the land itself, so the ברייתא teaches that they must still be protected.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it's needed for sheaves that still need the ground. You might have said that since they need the ground, they are like the ground itself. So it teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing a new point the ברייתא is teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sheaves that still depend on the ground might have been treated like the land, and so not covered by השבת אבידה. The ברייתא teaches that they are still separate objects that must be protected. This leaves the ברייתא saying nothing about land, so רבא's rule still has no proof from here.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for this specific case
It teaches us (that it is not so)

steps.whatToRemember: רבא says loss of land is included in השבת אבידה. The floodwater ברייתא is not proof, because it can be about sheaves that still need the ground, which still count as separate objects.

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where it has sheaves that still need the ground.
phrases.notes: The sheaves are still lying on the ground to dry.

phrases.english: You might have said:
since they need the ground,
they are like the ground itself,
so it teaches us that they are not.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא דְּאִית בַּהּ עוּמְרִין דִּצְרִיכִי לְאַרְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a special situation that teaches something new
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Sheaves that still need the ground might count like land and not need protecting
steps.terutzMaskana: Such sheaves are still separate objects and must be protected

steps.title: The משנה's first clause implies running or vineyard grazing is lost
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the משנה and says it contradicts itself. The first clause suggests that an animal running on the road, or grazing in vineyards, counts as lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'If one found a donkey or a cow, etc.' This itself is difficult! You said: a donkey or cow grazing on the road is not lost. So only grazing on the road is not lost, but running on the road or grazing among vineyards is lost.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new section on the משנה. It sets up a contradiction by reading what the first clause (רישא) implies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רישא lists only 'grazing on the road' as not lost. That suggests anything else counts as lost, including running on the road or grazing in vineyards. The next step will show the last clause suggests the opposite.

keyTerms.meaning: This itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)

phrases.english: If one found a donkey or a cow, etc.
This itself is difficult!
You said: If one found a donkey or a cow
grazing on the road, it is not a lost item.

phrases.aramaic: רוֹעִין בַּדֶּרֶךְ הוּא דְּלָא הָווּ אֲבֵידָה,
phrases.english: So only grazing on the road is not a lost item,
but running on the road
or grazing among the vineyards is a lost item.

steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of the משנה's first clause
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reading the רישא carefully, every case other than grazing on the road should count as lost

steps.title: The last clause implies the opposite
steps.stepSummary: The last clause (סיפא) lists only running in vineyards as lost. That suggests running on the road, or grazing in vineyards, is not lost, which clashes with the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now say the last clause: a donkey with its gear overturned, or a cow running among vineyards, is lost. So only running in vineyards is lost, but running on the road or grazing in vineyards is not lost!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the contradiction by reading what the סיפא implies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two middle cases, running on the road and grazing in vineyards, come out 'lost' from the רישא but 'not lost' from the סיפא. The משנה seems to contradict itself, and the גמרא will need to resolve this.
steps.confusionAlert: The fight is only about the two in-between cases: running on the road, and grazing in vineyards. Everyone agrees on grazing on the road (not lost) and running in vineyards (lost).

phrases.english: Say the last clause:
a donkey with its gear overturned

phrases.aramaic: וּפָרָה רָצָה בֵּין הַכְּרָמִים – הֲרֵי זוֹ אֲבֵידָה.
phrases.english: or a cow running among the vineyards, this is a lost item.

phrases.aramaic: רָצָה בֵּין הַכְּרָמִים הוּא דְּהָוְיָא אֲבֵידָה,
phrases.english: So only running among the vineyards is a lost item,
but running on the road

phrases.aramaic: וְרוֹעָה בֵּין הַכְּרָמִים – אֵין זוֹ אֲבֵידָה!
phrases.english: or grazing among the vineyards is not a lost item!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the contradiction begun in step 8
steps.kashyaTarget: The consistency of the משנה's רישא and סיפא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two clauses imply opposite rulings for the in-between cases

steps.title: אביי: each clause fills in the other
steps.stepSummary: אביי resolves the contradiction by saying the משנה teaches one example in each clause, and we must apply it to the parallel case too.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: the משנה works like 'its fellow tells about it.' It taught grazing on the road is not lost, and the same goes for grazing in vineyards. It taught running in vineyards is lost, and the same goes for running on the road.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the contradiction from steps 8–9. He says the משנה is not really splitting the cases differently; it just gave one example of each rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to אביי, the real dividing line is grazing versus running, not road versus vineyard. Grazing anywhere is not lost, and running anywhere is lost. The משנה mentioned one place for each and expects us to fill in the other, so the inferences that caused the contradiction are not real.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Its fellow tells about it': one case teaches us about its partner case

phrases.english: Abaye said: "Its fellow tells about it";
phrases.notes: A phrase from איוב 36:33. Here it means each clause of the משנה tells us about the other one.

phrases.english: he taught grazing on the road
that it is not a lost item,
and the same is true of grazing among the vineyards.
He taught running among the vineyards
that it is a lost item,
and the same is true of running on the road.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in steps 8–9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the משנה's style: each clause is one example that teaches about its partner.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each clause is listing exactly which cases count as lost, so the inferences contradict.
steps.terutzMaskana: The rule is grazing = not lost and running = lost, in any location. Each clause gives only one example.

steps.title: רבא: then the משנה should have picked the stronger examples
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects אביי's answer. If the משנה wanted one example to teach the other, it should have used the example that gives the 'all the more so' result.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: If it is 'its fellow tells about it,' let it teach the lighter case, and all the more so the stricter one. Let it teach that running on the road is lost, and all the more so running in vineyards. And let it teach that grazing in vineyards is not lost, and all the more so grazing on the road.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on אביי. If the משנה only gives one example, it should give the one that teaches the most.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Running on the road is the less obvious case of 'lost,' so if that is lost, running in vineyards surely is. Grazing in vineyards is the less obvious case of 'not lost,' so if that is fine, grazing on the road surely is. The משנה picked the weaker example in both clauses, so אביי's reading does not fit how a תנא normally teaches.

keyTerms.meaning: The lighter or less obvious case
The stricter or more obvious case
Let him teach (the משנה should have said)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Lighter' here does not mean 'more lenient' in the usual sense. It means the case where the rule is less obvious, so teaching the rule there teaches the most.

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
If it is "its fellow tells about it" –
let him teach the lighter case, and all the more so the stricter one.
Let him teach running on the road, that it is a lost item,
and all the more so running among the vineyards.
And let him teach grazing among the vineyards,
that it is not a lost item,
and all the more so grazing on the road.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רָבָא: אִי יַגִּיד עָלָיו רֵעוֹ לִיתְנֵי קִילְּתָא וְכׇל שֶׁכֵּן חֲמִירְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אביי's answer from step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects אביי's whole יגיד עליו רעו reading of the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A תנא who teaches one example for two cases would choose the less obvious one, so that 'all the more so' covers the other. The משנה did the opposite.

steps.title: Running: it depends which way the animal faces
steps.stepSummary: רבא resolves the running contradiction. An animal running on the road away from town is lost, and one running toward town is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: running against running is not difficult. This case is where it faces toward the field, and that case is where it faces toward the town.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own answer, starting with the contradiction about running on the road.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The רישא implied running on the road is lost. That is when the animal is heading away from town, toward the open field. The סיפא implied running on the road is not lost. That is when it is heading toward town, where it will likely get home. Both inferences are true, each for a different direction.

keyTerms.meaning: Its face (the direction it is facing)

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
Running against running is not difficult:
phrases.notes: He means the clash between what the רישא and the סיפא imply about running on the road.

phrases.english: this is where its face is toward the field,
phrases.notes: This is the רישא's case: heading away from town, so it counts as lost.

phrases.english: that is where its face is toward the town.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: רָצָה אַרָצָה לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting אביי, רבא gives a new answer to the contradiction from steps 8–9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the case (אוקימתא): the two clauses describe different situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Running on the road is one single case, so the רישא and the סיפא clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: Running on the road toward the field is lost. Running on the road toward town is not lost.

steps.title: Grazing: loss of the animal versus damage to the land
steps.stepSummary: רבא resolves the grazing contradiction. Grazing in vineyards does not make the animal itself lost, but one must still act because of the damage to the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: Grazing against grazing is also not difficult. Here it is about loss of the animal itself; there it is about loss to the land.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא finishes his answer by solving the second contradiction, about grazing in vineyards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The סיפא implied grazing in vineyards is not lost. That is true for the animal itself, which is safe and not going anywhere. The רישא implied grazing in vineyards is treated as lost. That is because of the damage the animal does to the vineyard's land. So both clauses are right, each about a different kind of loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Loss to the land (damage to the field)

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's full answer: running depends on direction (toward the field = lost, toward town = not lost). Grazing in vineyards is not a loss of the animal itself, but it counts because of damage to the land.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer connects the משנה back to the earlier topic of protecting land from loss (steps 3–7).

phrases.english: Grazing against grazing is also not difficult:
here it is about loss of the animal itself,
phrases.notes: This is the סיפא, which implied grazing in vineyards is not lost. The animal itself is safe.

phrases.english: there it is about loss to the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: רוֹעָה אַרוֹעָה נָמֵי לָא קַשְׁיָא כָּאן בַּאֲבֵידַת גּוּפָהּ כָּאן בַּאֲבֵידַת קַרְקַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's answer by handling the second half of the contradiction.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing two kinds of loss: the animal itself versus the land.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Grazing in vineyards must be either lost or not lost, so the two clauses clash.
steps.terutzMaskana: The animal itself is not lost, but the damage to the land is a loss that the רישא is concerned with.

steps.title: Two meanings of 'lost' explain both clauses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא spells out רבא's answer. The first clause speaks about damage to the land. The last clause speaks about danger to the animal itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: When the משנה says grazing on the road is not lost, it implies grazing in vineyards is lost. That means lost because of damage to the land. When it says running in vineyards is lost, it implies grazing in vineyards is not lost. That means the animal itself is not in danger, since running among vines gets the animal hurt and grazing does not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains in detail how רבא's answer fixes the clash between the two clauses of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each clause uses 'lost' in a different sense, so the two clauses no longer contradict each other. The first clause is about אבידת קרקע, harm to the vineyard. The last clause is about אבידת גופה, harm to the animal. A running animal gets cut by the vines, but a grazing animal does not.

keyTerms.meaning: Loss to the land: damage the animal does to the field or vineyard
Loss of the animal itself: danger to the animal
'But this': introduces what we learn by implication

steps.whatToRemember: Grazing in vineyards counts as 'lost' because of the damage to the land. It does not count as 'lost' because of danger to the animal.
steps.confusionAlert: Both clauses use the same word אבידה, but each clause means something different by it. Do not read the word the same way in both places.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי קָתָנֵי רוֹעָה בַּדֶּרֶךְ לָא הָוְיָא אֲבֵידָה,
phrases.english: When it teaches that an animal grazing on the road is not lost property,

phrases.aramaic: הָא רוֹעָה בֵּין הַכְּרָמִים הָוְיָא אֲבֵידָה
phrases.english: implying that one grazing among the vineyards is lost property,
that refers to loss of land.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי קָתָנֵי רָצָה בֵּין הַכְּרָמִים הָוְיָא אֲבֵידָה,
phrases.english: And when it teaches that one running among the vineyards is lost property,

phrases.aramaic: הָא רוֹעָה בֵּין הַכְּרָמִים לָא הָוְיָא אֲבֵידָה
phrases.english: implying that one grazing among the vineyards is not lost property,
that refers to loss of the animal itself,
since one running among the vineyards gets wounded,
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are the corrected spelling. Either way it means 'gets cut up' by the vines.

phrases.english: but one grazing among the vineyards does not get wounded.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי קָתָנֵי רוֹעָה בַּדֶּרֶךְ לָא הָוְיָא אֲבֵידָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the details of רבא's answer to the grazing contradiction from Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two different meanings of the same word
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two clauses seem to disagree about whether grazing among vineyards is lost.
steps.terutzMaskana: The first clause means loss to the land. The last clause means loss of the animal itself.

steps.title: Why not count grazing as lost because of the land?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about the last clause. Even if the grazing animal is not hurt, it should still count as lost because it damages the land.
steps.simpleTranslation: And as for an animal grazing among the vineyards: granted it does not get wounded, but it should count as lost because of the damage to the land!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the last clause. Why does it say grazing in vineyards is not lost at all, when the damage to the land should be enough to make it count?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 said that in the last clause, grazing is 'not lost' only in the sense that the animal is safe. But we already know grazing harms the land, which is a reason to act. So why would the משנה imply that you may ignore it?

keyTerms.meaning: 'Granted': admits one point before raising another
'Let it come out from': there should be another reason for the rule

phrases.english: And one grazing among the vineyards,
granted that it does not get wounded,
let it count as lost because of loss of land!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the last clause as Step 14 explained it.
steps.kashyaTarget: What we learn from the last clause: that grazing among vineyards is not lost
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Damage to the land is its own reason to act, so there should be a duty to act even if the animal is safe.

steps.title: The vineyard belongs to a גוי
steps.stepSummary: The last clause is talking about a vineyard that belongs to a גוי. There is no duty to protect a גוי's land.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about a vineyard of a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the last clause is talking about a vineyard owned by a גוי. So the damage to the land does not create a duty to act.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of אבידת קרקע only applies to protecting a Jew's land. Once the vineyard belongs to a גוי, that reason drops out. Only danger to the animal is left, and a grazing animal is not in danger.

phrases.english: With regard to that of a gentile.
phrases.notes: He means a vineyard owned by a non-Jew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case to a specific situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Damage to the land should require acting.
steps.terutzMaskana: The land belongs to a גוי, so there is no duty to protect it.

steps.title: But the גוי might kill the animal
steps.stepSummary: If the vineyard belongs to a גוי, the animal itself is in danger, because the גוי might kill it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let it count as lost because of danger to the animal itself, since perhaps they will kill it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own answer. If the vineyard belongs to a גוי, the animal is now in danger in a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying the vineyard belongs to a גוי removed the land reason. But it creates a new risk: an angry גוי owner might kill the trespassing animal. That would again make it אבידת גופה.

phrases.english: But let it count as lost because of loss of the animal itself,
since perhaps they will kill it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the vineyard belongs to a גוי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A גוי owner may kill the animal, so the animal itself is in danger.

steps.title: In this place they warn before killing
steps.stepSummary: The case is in a place where the vineyard owners first warn the animal's owner, and only then kill the animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about a place where they first warn, and only then kill.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that in this place the owners give a warning before they kill an animal. So the animal is not in danger right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because a warning comes first, the first time the animal grazes there it is not at risk of being killed. So there is still no אבידת גופה.

phrases.english: In a place where they warn and only then kill.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case to a specific situation
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The גוי might kill the animal right away.
steps.terutzMaskana: Here, a warning always comes first, so the animal is not in danger yet.

steps.title: Maybe the warning was already given
steps.stepSummary: Perhaps the owner was already warned, and now the animal could be killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps they already warned about it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges again. Maybe the warning was already given, which would put the animal in danger now.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in Step 18 only works if no warning has been given yet. If one was already given, the next step is killing, so the animal would be in danger.

phrases.english: But perhaps they already warned about it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in Step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that a warning comes before killing
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the warning was already given, the animal is now in real danger.

steps.title: Ignoring a warning means losing it on purpose
steps.stepSummary: If the owner was warned and did not take care, he lost the animal on purpose (אבידה מדעת). There is no duty to return that.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they warned about it and he did not take care, this is certainly losing it on purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that an owner who ignored the warning lost the animal on purpose. That ends this back-and-forth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Either no warning was given, so the animal is safe for now, or a warning was given and ignored. In that second case it is אבידה מדעת, which the finder does not have to return. Either way, the last clause is right that grazing here is not a lost item you must deal with.

keyTerms.meaning: Something lost on purpose: no duty to return it

steps.whatToRemember: The last clause is about a גוי's vineyard. No warning means the animal is safe for now. A warning that was ignored means the owner lost it on purpose (אבידה מדעת). Either way, there is no duty to return it.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתְרוֹ בַּהּ וְלָא אִזְדְּהַרוּ בַּהּ,
phrases.english: If they warned about it and they did not take care of it,
it is certainly a loss done knowingly.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אַתְרוֹ בַּהּ וְלָא אִזְדְּהַרוּ בַּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 19 and closes the discussion about grazing among vineyards.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Once a warning was given, the animal is in danger and must be saved.
steps.terutzMaskana: Ignoring the warning makes it a loss done on purpose, so there is no duty to return it.

steps.title: Quoting the next line of the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of an animal that is returned and keeps running away.
steps.simpleTranslation: He returned it and it ran away, he returned it and it ran away, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the next discussion. The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that you must keep returning an animal even if it keeps running away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה learns from the double wording 'השב תשיבם' (דברים 22:1) that you must return the animal many times. The next step will question how many times this really means.

phrases.english: He returned it and it ran away, he returned it and it ran away, etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' points to the rest of the משנה line: even four or five times, he must return it, because it says 'השב תשיבם'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You must keep returning an animal that keeps running away.

steps.title: Maybe the double wording means only twice
steps.stepSummary: A חכם suggests to רבא that 'השב' means once and 'תשיבם' means twice, and no more.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of the חכמים said to רבא: Say that 'השב' means one time and 'תשיבם' means two times!
steps.whatsHappening: A חכם challenges the משנה's reading of the פסוק. He suggests that the two words only require returning the animal twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says there is no limit. This חכם argues that each word adds just one more return, so the total should stop at two. The question is whether the double wording means 'many times' or exactly 'two times'.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You shall surely return them' (דברים 22:1): the word is doubled

phrases.english: A certain one of the Sages said to Rava:
Say that 'return' means one time,
phrases.notes: דברים 22:1

phrases.english: and 'you shall return them' means two times!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִדְּרַבָּנַן לְרָבָא אֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how the משנה reads the פסוק from Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that there is no limit to how many times you must return it
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The doubled verb can be read as just two separate commands, which would mean only two returns.

steps.title: רבא: Return Even a Hundred Times, and to the Garden or Ruin Too
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that השב alone already means an unlimited number of returns. תשיבם teaches a different point: returning the animal to the owner's garden or ruin also counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: "Return" means even a hundred times. From "you shall return them" I would only know to return it to his house. How do I know that returning it to his garden or his ruin counts? The verse says "you shall return them," meaning in any place.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects the חכם's idea that the two words mean 'once' and 'twice.' He gives each word its own job.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכם read the doubled verb as a way of counting returns. רבא says the first word, השב, already means 'keep returning, no matter how many times.' The second word, תשיבם, is free to teach something new: it widens the places where a return counts, beyond the owner's house.

keyTerms.meaning: Return (the first word of the doubled verb)
You shall return them (the second word)
In any case or in any place

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think השב means 'once.' According to רבא, the 'hundred times' rule comes from השב alone. תשיבם is about WHERE you return the animal, not how many times.

phrases.english: He said to him: "Return"
phrases.notes: This is רבא answering the חכם from the last step.

phrases.english: implies even a hundred times.
"You shall return them": I would only know to his house.
To his garden and to his ruin, from where do we know?
The verse says "you shall return them," meaning in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: ״הָשֵׁב״ אֲפִילּוּ מֵאָה פְּעָמִים מַשְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the חכם's challenge from step 22
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives each word of the doubled verb its own separate teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: השב means one return and תשיבם means a second return, and no more.
steps.terutzMaskana: השב means unlimited returns, and תשיבם means a return to the garden or ruin also counts.

steps.title: What Kind of Garden or Ruin Is Meant?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case רבא means. If the garden is protected, the rule is obvious. If it is not protected, why would leaving the animal there count as returning it?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the place is guarded, it is obvious. If it is not guarded, why should it count?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the teaching of תשיבם by asking what case it could be talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both options seem to fail. A protected place is just like the house, so why would we need a verse for it? An unprotected place leaves the animal free to run off again, so it should not count as a return at all.

keyTerms.meaning: What are the circumstances? What is the case?

phrases.english: What is the case?
If it is guarded, it is obvious.
If it is not guarded, why should it count?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the teaching of תשיבם from step 23
steps.kashyaTarget: The teaching that returning the animal to the garden or ruin counts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both possible cases fail: a protected place makes the verse unnecessary, and an unprotected place should not count as a return.

steps.title: A Protected Place, and the Owner Does Not Need to Know
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is a protected garden or ruin. The new point is that the owner does not have to know the animal was returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Really it is a guarded place. And this teaches us that we do not need the owner to know.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא takes the 'protected place' option and explains what new lesson the verse adds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new point is not that a protected place is safe; that much is obvious. When you put the animal in the owner's house, he will probably see it. In a garden or ruin he may not know it is there, and the verse teaches that the return still counts.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it teaches us

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a practical rule: you can complete a lost-item return without telling the owner, as long as the item is safely back in his protected property.

phrases.english: Really, it is where the place is guarded.
And this is what it teaches us:
that we do not need the owner's knowledge.

steps.triggerLanguage: לְעוֹלָם דְּמִינַּטְרָא, וְהָא קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Picks one side of the dilemma and shows it teaches something that is not obvious
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A protected garden is obvious, so the verse would add nothing.
steps.terutzMaskana: The verse teaches that the return counts even though the owner does not know about it.

steps.title: This Fits the View of רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא shows that this rule matches רבי אלעזר. He says every other kind of returning needs the owner's knowledge, but returning a lost item does not, because the Torah widened the ways to return it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is like רבי אלעזר, who said: Every return needs the owner's knowledge, except returning a lost item, because the Torah added many kinds of returning.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא supports the answer of step 25 by connecting it to a known statement of רבי אלעזר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אלעזר states a general rule: giving something back normally requires the owner to know about it. A lost item is the exception. He explains that the doubled verb השב תשיבם 'widened' the kinds of returns that count, and returning without the owner's knowledge is one of them.
steps.whatToRemember: השב means returning even a hundred times. תשיבם means a return to a protected garden or ruin counts, even without the owner knowing, just as רבי אלעזר said.

phrases.english: And this is like רבי אלעזר, who said:
Everyone needs the owner's knowledge,
phrases.notes: He means anyone giving something back to its owner. Normally the owner has to know it was returned.

phrases.english: except for returning a lost item,
because the Torah included many kinds of returning.
phrases.notes: This points to the doubled verb הָשֵׁב תְּשִׁיבֵם.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of step 25 with an earlier statement
steps.raayaObject: The rule that returning a lost item does not need the owner's knowledge
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי אלעזר's statement that only returning a lost item is free of the need for the owner's knowledge

steps.title: Same Question on Sending Away the Mother Bird
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the same question about שלח תשלח. Maybe שלח means sending the mother bird away once and תשלח means twice, and no more.
steps.simpleTranslation: "You shall surely send away": say that "send away" means one time and "you shall send away" means two times!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to another מצוה with a doubled verb and asks the same 'once and twice' question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This challenge works exactly like the חכם's question in step 22. If doubled verbs just count actions, then you would only have to send away the mother bird twice.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall surely send away (the mother bird)

phrases.english: "You shall surely send away":
phrases.notes: דברים 22:7, about sending away the mother bird before taking the eggs or chicks.

phrases.english: say that "send away" means one time,
and "you shall send away" means two times!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the challenge of step 22 for a different מצוה
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that sending away the mother bird has no limit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The doubled verb may only count two sendings, not an unlimited number.

steps.title: Send Away Even a Hundred Times, Even for a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers the same way. שלח already means even a hundred times. תשלח teaches that you must send away the mother bird even when you need it for a מצוה, not only for an optional use.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: "Send away" means even a hundred times. From "you shall send away" I would only know for an optional matter. How do I know it applies for a מצוה matter? The verse says "you shall send away," meaning in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the same way he did for lost items. The first word means unlimited times, and the second word widens the rule to a new case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as with השב תשיבם, the first word already covers 'every time it comes back.' The second word teaches that even when the bird is needed for a מצוה, you still have to send it away. One might have thought a מצוה need would override the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: An optional matter, such as wanting to eat the bird

steps.whatToRemember: Both doubled verbs follow the same pattern. The first word means unlimited times, and the second word widens the rule: to a garden or ruin for a lost item, and to a מצוה need for the mother bird.

phrases.english: He said to him: "Send away"
implies even a hundred times.
"You shall send away": I would only know for an optional matter.
For a מצוה matter, from where do we know?
The verse says "you shall send away," meaning in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: ״שַׁלֵּחַ״ אֲפִילּוּ מֵאָה פְּעָמִים מַשְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 27 using the same method as step 23
steps.terutzResolutionType: Gives each word of the doubled verb its own separate teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שלח means once and תשלח means twice.
steps.terutzMaskana: שלח means unlimited times, and תשלח extends the obligation to a case where the bird is needed for a מצוה.

steps.title: Does הוכח תוכיח mean only once and twice?
steps.stepSummary: One of the חכמים challenges רבא: maybe the doubled verb for rebuke limits the duty to two times.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of the חכמים said to רבא: Maybe הוכח means rebuke once, and תוכיח means rebuke a second time, and no more?
steps.whatsHappening: One of the חכמים raises the same kind of challenge we saw with returning a lost item and with שלח תשלח, now about the מצוה of rebuke.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse says הוכח תוכיח, using the same verb twice. This חכם suggests each word counts as one time, so the doubling would set a limit of two rebukes. If that were true, the duty to rebuke would stop after the second time.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall surely rebuke (the doubled verb in ויקרא 19:17)
A certain one of the scholars

phrases.english: A certain one of the scholars said to Rava:
But say that "hokheach" means one time,
phrases.notes: The פסוק is ויקרא 19:17, about rebuking someone who does wrong.

phrases.english: and "tokhiach" means two times?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same once-or-twice challenge from שלח תשלח to a new doubled verb.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that the doubled verb הוכח תוכיח requires unlimited rebuke
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each word of the doubled verb could stand for one time, which would cap the duty at two rebukes.

steps.title: Rebuke even a hundred times, and a student rebukes his teacher too
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that הוכח alone means unlimited times, and תוכיח teaches that a student must also rebuke his teacher.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to him: הוכח by itself means even a hundred times. תוכיח teaches something else. I might have known only that a teacher rebukes a student. How do we know a student must rebuke a teacher? The verse says הוכח תוכיח, meaning in every case.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the same kind of answer he gave before. The first word already means no limit, so the second word must teach something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verb הוכח already means you keep rebuking, even a hundred times, so the second word is not needed to count times. It is used instead to widen who must rebuke whom. Not only a teacher rebuking a student, but also a student rebuking his teacher.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case / in every situation

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that the duty of תוכחה does not depend on rank. Even a student must rebuke his teacher when it is needed.

phrases.english: He said to him:
"Hokheach" means even one hundred times.
"Tokhiach": I would only know a teacher rebuking a student.
A student rebuking a teacher, from where do we know it?
The verse says: "hokheach tokhiach," meaning in any case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 29 using the same method as step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reassigns the second word to a new lesson instead of a count
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The doubled verb limits rebuke to two times.
steps.terutzMaskana: One word already means unlimited times. The doubling adds that a student must rebuke his teacher too.

steps.title: Unloading a fallen animal even when the owner is not there
steps.stepSummary: The doubled verb עזב תעזב teaches that you must help unload an animal even if its owner is absent.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says עזב תעזב עמו, "you shall surely help unload with him." I would only know this when the owner is with the animal. How do we know it applies when the owner is not with it? The verse says עזב תעזב, meaning in every case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another example of a doubled verb, this time about helping unload a donkey that fell under its load.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word עמו ("with him") suggests you only help when the owner is there working with you. The doubled verb widens the מצוה so it applies even when the owner is not present.

keyTerms.meaning: The מצוה of unloading a fallen animal

phrases.english: "You shall surely release it with him":
phrases.notes: שמות 23:5. This is about helping unload a donkey that collapsed under its load.

phrases.english: I would only know when its owner is with it.
When its owner is not with it, from where do we know?
The verse says "azov ta'azov," meaning in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״עָזֹב תַּעֲזֹב עִמּוֹ״, אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בְּעָלָיו עִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another doubled-verb lesson in the same style as הוכח תוכיח.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The duty to help unload a fallen animal applies even when the owner is not there.

steps.title: Loading an animal even when the owner is not there
steps.stepSummary: The doubled verb הקם תקים teaches that you must help load an animal even if its owner is absent.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse says הקם תקים עמו, "you shall surely lift it with him." I would only know this when the owner is with the animal. How do we know it applies when the owner is not with it? The verse says הקם תקים, meaning in every case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives one more doubled verb, now about helping lift the load back onto a fallen animal. It follows the same pattern as the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again the word עמו could limit the מצוה to times when the owner is helping. The doubled verb shows that you must help load even without the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: You shall surely lift it up (דברים 22:4)
The מצוה of helping load an animal

steps.whatToRemember: Every doubled verb here follows one pattern. The first word covers the basic rule (even many times), and the doubling widens the מצוה. For rebuke, a student must rebuke his teacher too. For unloading and loading, you must help even when the owner is not there.

phrases.english: "You shall surely lift them with him":
phrases.notes: דברים 22:4. This is about helping put the load back onto the animal.

phrases.english: I would only know when its owner is with it.
When its owner is not with it, from where do we know?
The verse says "hakem takim," meaning in any case.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״הָקֵם תָּקִים עִמּוֹ״, אֵין לִי אֶלָּא בְּעָלָיו עִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel to step 31, applying the same lesson to loading instead of unloading.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The duty to help load an animal applies even when the owner is not there.

steps.title: Why teach the owner-absent rule for both unloading and loading?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the Torah needed doubled verbs for both פריקה and טעינה. It could have taught the rule once and let us learn the other case from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why did the Torah need to write this for unloading, and why did it need to write it for loading?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the two teachings from steps 31–32. It asks why the Torah repeated the rule for both cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah does not waste words. If helping without the owner applies to unloading, we might simply have applied it to loading too, or the other way around. So the גמרא asks why both are written.

keyTerms.meaning: Unloading a burden off an animal
Loading a burden back onto an animal
Why does it need to write? (a question about extra wording)

phrases.english: And why does it need to write unloading,
phrases.notes: This is about the doubled verbs from steps 31–32, which teach that you help even when the owner isn't there.

phrases.english: and why does it need to write loading?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for both derivations given in steps 31 and 32.
steps.kashyaTarget: Having two separate derivations for פריקה and טעינה when the owner is absent
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: One verse should be enough, since the other case could be learned from it.

steps.title: Unloading alone would not teach loading
steps.stepSummary: Both verses are needed. Unloading involves animal suffering and money loss. Loading has neither, so we would not have learned it from unloading.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both are needed. If the Torah had written only unloading, I would have said that is because there is animal suffering and money loss. But loading has no animal suffering and no money loss, so I would say there is no duty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with צריכי, meaning both are needed. This is the first half of the answer: why unloading alone would not be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An overloaded animal is suffering (צער בעלי חיים), and the animal or its load may be ruined (חסרון כיס). Loading lacks both of these urgent reasons. So we might have thought there is no duty to load when the owner is absent.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
I would have said (a mistaken first thought)

phrases.english: They are needed, for if the Merciful One had written unloading,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה אָמֵינָא מִשּׁוּם דְּאִיכָּא צַעַר בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים
phrases.english: I would have said it is because there is suffering of animals
and there is money loss,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל טְעִינָה, דְּלָאו צַעַר בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים אִיכָּא
phrases.english: but loading, where there is no suffering of animals

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא חֶסְרוֹן כִּיס אִיכָּא, אֵימָא לָא.
phrases.english: and there is no money loss, I would say no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 33.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each case has a unique feature
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only unloading would require help without the owner, because of animal suffering and money loss.

steps.title: Loading alone would not teach unloading
steps.stepSummary: If only loading were written, we would think the duty exists because the helper gets paid. Unloading is done for free, so it needs its own verse.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the Torah had taught only loading, I would say that is because it is done for pay. But unloading, which is done for free, I would say no. So both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the צריכי answer. It shows why loading alone would not be enough, and the גמרא concludes that both are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each case has something the other lacks. Unloading has urgency, and loading has payment. So neither could be learned from the other.
steps.whatToRemember: פריקה is urgent (animal suffering and money loss) but unpaid. טעינה is paid but not urgent. Each has a reason the other lacks, so both are written.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us loading, it would be because it is for pay,
but unloading, which is for free, I would say no.
So it is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the צריכי answer that began in step 34.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only loading would require help without the owner, because the helper is paid.

steps.title: How does this work for רבי שמעון?
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון holds that loading is also done for free. Then the 'pay' reason disappears, so why would unloading need its own verse?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to רבי שמעון, who says even loading is for free, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the second half of the answer (step 35) from the view of רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 35 said loading has something special: payment. For רבי שמעון loading is also free. So unloading has everything loading has and more, and it seems one verse should be enough.

keyTerms.meaning: What is there to say? (how can we answer?)

phrases.aramaic: וּלְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן דְּאָמַר: אַף טְעִינָה בְּחִנָּם,
phrases.english: And according to רבי שמעון, who says: even loading is for free,
what is there to say?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning of step 35 according to another view.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If loading is also free, it has no special feature, so unloading could have been learned from it.

steps.title: For רבי שמעון the verses are not clearly marked
steps.stepSummary: For רבי שמעון, we could not tell which verse is about loading and which is about unloading. So both are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to רבי שמעון, the verses are not clearly defined.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that for רבי שמעון the two verses are not clearly marked as loading or unloading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only one verse were written, we would read it as being about unloading. Then we would not know that the owner-absent rule also applies to loading. Writing both verses makes sure both cases are covered.

keyTerms.meaning: The verses are not clearly defined (which is about what)

phrases.english: According to רבי שמעון, the verses are not clearly defined.
phrases.notes: He means: nothing in the verses marks which one is about loading and which one is about unloading.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 36.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading of the verses: we cannot tell which verse is which
steps.terutzHavaAmina: For רבי שמעון one verse would be enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבי שמעון both verses are needed, because one verse alone would be read as being about unloading only.

steps.title: Why write both the animal מצוות and returning a lost item?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks a broader question. Why does the Torah need both the animal מצוות (unloading and loading) and the מצוה of returning a lost item?
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need it to write these two, and why do I need it to write a lost item?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא widens the question. It asks why the Torah needs both פריקה and טעינה and also השבת אבידה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All of these מצוות are about protecting another Jew's property. So it seems one could have been learned from the other.

keyTerms.meaning: A lost item (the מצוה to return it)

phrases.english: Why do I need it to write these two,
and why do I need it to write a lost item?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from comparing loading and unloading to comparing both of them with אבידה.
steps.kashyaTarget: Having separate מצוות for the animal cases and for אבידה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: All are מצוות of protecting a friend's property, so one should teach the other.

steps.title: The animal מצוות would not teach returning a lost item
steps.stepSummary: Unloading and loading involve suffering for both the owner and the animal. A lost item causes suffering only to its owner, so we would not learn אבידה from them.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are needed. If the Torah had written only these two, I would say it is because there is the owner's suffering and the animal's own suffering. But a lost item, where there is the owner's suffering but no suffering of the item itself, I would say no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers צריכי again. This first half explains why the animal מצוות alone would not teach אבידה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the animal cases two people, so to speak, are hurting: the owner and the animal. With a lost object only the owner is hurting, so it is a weaker case. We might have thought there is no duty to return it.

phrases.aramaic: צְרִיכִי, דְּאִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא הָנֵי תַּרְתֵּי –
phrases.english: They are needed, for if the Merciful One had written these two,
it would be because there is the suffering of its owner,
and there is its own suffering.
But a lost item, where there is the suffering of its owner
but there is no suffering of its own, I would say no.

steps.triggerLanguage: צְרִיכִי, דְּאִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא הָנֵי תַּרְתֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 38.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each case has a unique feature
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only the animal cases would carry a duty, since both the owner and the animal suffer.

steps.title: Starting the other side: a lost item has no owner with it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins the second half. If only אבידה were written, we would say the duty exists because the owner is not with his item. The rest of the answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it had taught us only a lost item, I would say that is because its owner is not with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up the second half of the צריכי answer. It shows why אבידה alone would not teach the animal מצוות, and the conclusion comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A lost item is helpless, because no owner is there to look after it. This is a special reason that might apply only to אבידה. The text that follows will explain why the animal cases, where the owner may be present, are different.

phrases.english: And if it had taught us a lost item,
it would be because its owner is not with it,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the second side of the צריכי answer that began in step 39.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: second side (continues on the next amud)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only אבידה would carry a duty, since the owner is not there to protect his property.
